content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper deals with the problem of early diagnosis of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) from medical image-derived phenotypes. 
The problem is relevant from a medical viewpoint and falls within the scope of the conference as a practical application of existing ML methods.
The use of image-derived phenotypic data is novel enough and probably important from a practical perspective, as it would avoid costly/invasive blood lab measurements. Beyond standard classification, authors propose the novel use of the obtained models as the basis for what they call ‘SynthA1c encoders’ to provide a "synthetic estimate of patient blood hemoglobin A1C". 
Authors also show that the use of the T2DM risk prediction model sensitivity to small perturbations of the input could be used to guarantee generalization capabilities with unseen test data.
The premise of the whole study is somehow unusual from a practical clinical standpoint, because it suggests to "estimate patient risk of T2DM as an incidental finding during an outpatient imaging appointment". That is, using medical images that could have been obtained for a completely different purpose in order to implement a sort of preventive screening for T2DM early detection. Not sure to what extent this "incidental finding" expedition would be allowed in practice.
Section 2.2, concerning "related work in classification methods" would require a more clear distinction between classifiers that have previously been used to tackle the same or similar problem, and classifiers in general. Specifically, I would appreciate a more systematic description and details of models that have been used in the same problem.
Classifiers were evaluated based on recall, precision, specificity, and overall accuracy. Why not AUC, which would be far more standard and robust? Why not sensitivity, together with the already calculated specificity?
The dataset is class-unbalanced. Do authors reckon this may have affected performance? Results in table 2 may suggest so, specially with DM + Pre-DM classification.
Authors do not clarify with enough clarity why do they use supervised encoder models in order to predict HbA1c values from feature inputs.
In order to find out "which input features are most important for classification performance?" (section 5.4), why did authors decided not to use feature selection / relevance determination approaches?
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper examines the use of CT image-derived phenotype (IDP) data, towards predicting patient Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) risk. The main benefit is the exploitation of CT scans possibly acquired for other tests, to predict (or improve the prediction) of T2DM. Towards this, r-Models (with raw feature inputs) and p-Models (with raw features combined into composite features, e.g. BMI from height and weight) are validated. Furthermore, the paper proposes a synthetic estimate of patient HbA1c (SynthA1c) to improve clinical interpretability of the model predictions, and also a model smoothness metric to improve T2DM risk stratification on unseen, out-of-domain patient datasets. In general, it appears that IDP input allows improved performance compared to models trained with commonly-used clinically-derived phenotype (CDP) data only (Table 6).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. Results suggest that combining both IDPs with CDPs can further improve the performance of T2DM prediction models.

2. Hyperparameter and experiment details are comprehensively stated in the Appendix.

3. Detailed stratification analysis provided in the Appendix.

Possible Weaknesses/Considerations:

4. In Section 3, it is stated that patients with any missing values were excluded. The number of such exclusions might be presented (possibly in a flowchart), along with patient demographics if possible.

5. In Section 3, it is stated that the final dataset consisted of 389 patients with 2077 HbA1c measurements.  This implies that a patient is represented by multiple HbA1c measurement in the dataset (also Figure 1). It might then be clarified as to whether the 208 randomly selected test samples were stratified at the patient level, or whether a patient may have his data present in both the training and test subsets.

6. It is stated that an axial border classification network and fat segmentation network are used to estimate the IDPs. The accuracy/reliability of these networks might thus be described.

7. P-metrics do not appear explored for the results described in Table 2.

8. The implications of using raw vs. processed features (in r- and p-Models respectively) are not very clearly presented; Section 5.2 and Table 3 suggests that this makes little difference, also when their union (both r- and p- features) are used. This might be expected to an extent since the raw features technically allow the respective processed features to be derived.  In general, a feature importance analysis for individual features might be more illuminating.

9. The set of classifiers examined are not consistent across various experiments (e.g. DM classification in Table 2, SynthA1c classification in Table 3). This does not allow for a complete comparison. 

10. For the prediction of SynthA1c values, it is stated that traditional HbA1c threshold values were then used for the T2DM/pre-diabetes prediction. It might be clarified if any (bias) adjustment had been performed for the SynthA1c value prediction, possibly using a validation dataset.

11. The comparison between models/classifiers in the main results (Table 2, 3, 6) involves only metrics at a single operating threshold (recall, precision, specificity, accuracy); this leads to trivial models such as Zero-Rule seemingly outperforming, depending on the metrics considered (the claim that “All DNN models outperformed the Zero-Rule and Weighted Random baselines” in Section 5.1 is not obvious from the results tables). Metrics such as AUROC/AUPRC might be reported too, to more fully characterize the performance of the various classifiers.

12. The local manifold smoothing for out-of-domain characterization appears to return inconsistent results with the OOD datasets used, with the hypothesis that smoother models generalize better to unseen datasets holding for only one of the two OOD datasets. Moreover, the value of the smoothing metric is unclear; is it actionable towards improving predictive performance/adjusting the results?

13. In Section 5.4, it is claimed that “In contrast, our classifiers presented herein are the first to incorporate IDPs as input model features”. This claim might be made more specific with respect to prior work, e.g. Tallam et al (2022). Fully Automated Abdominal CT Biomarkers for Type 2 Diabetes Using Deep Learning. Radiology, 211914.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The methodology is largely clearly described, with a few missing details as mentioned in the Strength and Weaknesses section. The technical novelty appears relatively limited, with processed features known in the literature, SynthA1c largely predicting the continuous HbA1c value instead of a discrete diabetes class, and local manifold smoothness metric also heavily inspired by prior work. Experiments appear reproducible with training details provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper explores IDPs, continuous HbA1c prediction and local manifold smoothness as a way of characterizing out-of-domain model performance, for T2DM prediction. While likely of practical interest, there remain concerns about the technical novelty involved, and the metrics used to describe model performance.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors proposed to utilize both the clinically derived phenotypes and image-derived ones for the prediction of type 2 diabetes mellitus. A list of DNN and decision tree models are adopted as the classifier, while input features are grouped into clinically derived and image-derived phenotypes. A private dataset with 389 patients and overly 2k samples is employed for the experiments. Superior classification results are reported when both groups of features are utilized, and the HbA1c measurements can be accurately predicted using the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The authors investigated the power of image-based radiomic features compared to clinical data and demonstrated a combination of both will provide the best classification power.

Weakness:
- I will recommend the authors submit the presented work to a more clinical-application-oriented journal/conference since the technical innovation in the presented work is limited. It largely leverages the existing techniques and mainly investigates the features/phenotypes of type 2 diabetes mellitus. 

- The sections could be reorganized. For example, the modeling parts presented in the Results section should be moved to the Method section. In addition, the detailed setting of the classification models should be introduced. It is also not clear how the features are organized and combined together as inputs to the models.

- What's DM+pre-DM as shown in Tables 2 and 6?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Many of the details in the proposed approach are not well-presented, and some parts need to be reorganized.
- The technical novelty of the proposed method is minimal.
- The code is provided for the reproducing purpose
content.summary_of_the_review: My primary concern is the presented work does not fit the scope of ICLR very well due to its more application-oriented contents. Furthermore, the clarity of the manuscript could be largely improved.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents experiment results on using clinically derived phenotypes (CDPs) and image-derived phenotypes (IDPs) to predict Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

Significant implication for early diagnosis of T2DM and potential early interventions. 

Weaknesses

1) It's unclear how IDPs are generated. The authors describe that "the dataset consists of over 60K patients from the Anonymized Institution Health System mapped to over 10K ICD-9 codes". Is image phenotype derivation part of the presented work? Or the authors take this structured data from others?

2) I'm having a hard time digesting Eq. (3). Is this a distance measure between $\hat{x}\_{ij}$ and $\hat{d}_{ij}$? But x is the measurement and d is time. Why do we want to measure their distance?

3) I can't find in the main sections (first 8 pages) how the classification cutoff is chosen. Area under the curve (AUC) should be reported along with accuracy.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: High clarify and quality, but lack of novelty in methodology or mathematical modeling.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this type of work is important for advancing early diagnosis and enabling early interventions for T2DM. But due to the lack of methodological or mathematical modeling innovations, this paper could be more appreciated in a different community.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Comments
content.comment:
We thank all of the reviewers for their insightful and valuable feedback and taking the time to read through our work. We appreciate that many of the reviewers share our enthusiasm for our proposed approach in estimating patient risk of T2DM may prove useful in future clinical applications.

To summarize the concerns raised, there were a few equations and arguments made in our manuscript that could benefit from additional clarification. Many of the reviewers raised a good point that our classification metrics presented in Table 2 of the text would benefit from reporting AUROC measurements as well, which are currently included in Figure B1 in the Appendix. There were also some improvements to be made regarding the clarity of some of the points made in the main text and figures. We appreciate these feedback and have updated our manuscript in accordance with these comments.

The primary concern raised by many of the reviewers was that our manuscript may be outside of the scope of the work traditionally presented at ICLR. Given the collective feedback presented, we agree with the reviewers' assessment that our work may be better appreciated by readership of other applications-based and/or medical research journals. Therefore, we have decided to withdraw our submission from consideration in this year's ICLR conference.

Thank you again to the reviewers and area chairs for taking the time to evaluate and improve our work!
